SUMMARY OF:
Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 on horizontal cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements
WHAT IS THE AIM OF THE REGULATION?
Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), aims to strengthen cybersecurity across the European Union (EU). It sets out a comprehensive framework to ensure that digital products and services are:
secure by design;
resilient against cyber threats; and
capable of providing continuing protection throughout their life cycle.
It addresses the growing cybersecurity challenges posed by the increasing connectivity of devices and the rise in the number of cyberattacks, which have significant economic and societal impacts.
KEY POINTS
The CRA has several core objectives:
enhance cybersecurity across the EU by setting mandatory cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements;
promote secure practices by encouraging manufacturers to integrate cybersecurity into the product design and development phases;

Cyber Resilience Act
The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) aims to make sure all digital products are safe from cyber threats. This rulebook requires that devices and software are designed, updated, and maintained to protect users in our increasingly digital world.
From baby-monitors to smart watches, from apps to computer programs, connectable hardware and software are omnipresent in our daily lives. Less apparent to many users is the security risk such products may present.
The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) aims to safeguard consumers and businesses buying software or hardware products with digital elements. The CRA addresses the inadequate level of cybersecurity in many products, and the lack of timely security updates. It also tackles the challenges consumers and businesses currently face when trying to determining which products are cybersecure and in setting them up securely, making it easier to identify hardware and software with the proper cybersecurity features.

quotes.whole:
The CRA introduces mandatory cybersecurity requirements for manufacturers, covering the planning, design, development and maintenance of such products. These obligations must be met at every stage of the value chain. The CRA also requires manufacturers to handle vulnerabilities during the lifecycle of their products. Some products of particular relevance for cybersecurity may need to undergo a third-party assessment by a notified body before they are sold on the EU market.
Products will bear the CE marking to indicate that they comply with the CRA requirements and national market surveillance authorities will ensure enforcement of the rules.
The CRA entered into force on 10 December 2024. The main obligations introduced by the Act will apply from 11 December 2027, with reporting obligations to apply as of 11 September 2026.
On 27 July 2026, the Commission published practical guidance to help manufacturers, developers, and businesses of all sizes meet their obligations under the Cyber Resilience Act.
The Cyber Resilience Act builds on the 2020 EU Cybersecurity Strategy and EU Security Union Strategy. It complements other legislation in this area, specifically the NIS2 Directive.

Under the CRA, manufacturers placing on the EU market products with digital elements are required to notify two specific types of events:
Actively Exploited Vulnerabilities: vulnerabilities in products with digital elements for which there is reliable evidence that they have been exploited by a malicious actor;
Severe Incidents: incidents having a severe impact on the security of a product with digital elements (e.g., compromising its availability, authenticity, integrity, or confidentiality). The criteria for severity are set out in Art. 14(5).

quotes.whole:
7. What are the deadlines for reporting?
The reporting process starts when a manufacturer or open-source steward becomes aware of an actively exploited vulnerability or severe incident.
‘Actively exploited vulnerability’ means a vulnerability for which there is reliable evidence that a malicious actor has exploited it in a system without permission of the system owner (CRA definition).
‘Incident having an impact on the security of the product with digital elements’ means an incident that negatively affects (or is capable of negatively affecting) the ability of a product with digital elements to protect the availability, authenticity, integrity or confidentiality of data or functions (CRA definition).
Manufacturers and, once applicable, open-source software stewards must adhere to the following reporting deadlines:
Early Warning: Without undue delay and in any case within 24 hours of becoming aware of the actively exploited vulnerability or severe incident;
Actively Exploited Vulnerability/Severe Incident Notification: Without undue delay and in any case within 72 hours of becoming aware, providing general information and an initial assessment;

From 11 September 2026 on, the reporting obligations under the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) will apply. These apply to manufacturers of products with digital elements as defined by the CRA who make their products available on the European Union (EU) internal market. Reporting is required for actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents affecting the security of products with digital elements.

quotes.whole:
Note
Please note that there is no obligation to register before a report needs to be submitted via the CRA Single Reporting Platform (CRA-SRP).
CRA-SRP registration and submission of reports can be completed within a few minutes if required.
Definition of the two reporting categories
The following definitions apply to the classification of events subject to reporting under the CRA.
Actively exploited vulnerability
In accordance with Article 3 (42) of the CRA, this is a vulnerability for which there is reliable evidence that a malicious actor has demonstrably exploited it in a system without permission.
The following two conditions must be met for a vulnerability to be subject to mandatory reporting:
The vulnerability is present in a product with digital elements.
There is credible evidence of actual exploitation in real-world systems.
A published exploit (code to exploit the vulnerability), proof-of-concept code or port scans are not sufficient. A vulnerability that is theoretically exploitable but not actively exploited is not subject to the CRA reporting obligation.

Reporting deadlines
Under Article 14 (2) (actively exploited vulnerability) and Article 14 (3) (severe incident), the following deadlines apply to the sequential reporting stages:
An early warning must be issued within 24 hours following reliable information received by the manufacturer regarding an actively exploited vulnerability or a severe incident affecting products with digital elements.
A more detailed report within 72 hours.

out a cybersecurity risk assessment of a product with digital elements and take the results of that
assessment into account during the planning, design, development, production, delivery and maintenance
phases of the product with digital elements, with a view to minimising cybersecurity risks, preventing
incidents and minimising their impact, including on the health and safety of users.
The cybersecurity risk assessment will be documented and updated during a support period. When
placing a product with digital elements on the market, the manufacturer will ensure that vulnerabilities in
that product are managed effectively and in accordance with the essential requirements. When identifying
a vulnerability in a component, including an open-source software component, that is integrated into the
product with digital elements, the manufacturer will report the vulnerability to the person or entity that
maintains the component, and address and remediate the vulnerability.

verdict.summary:
REGULATORY ANALYSIS — EU CYBER RESILIENCE ACT, ART. 14 REPORTING
Facts: connected consumer product placed on the EU market in 2025; manufacturer becomes aware on 17 November 2026 that a vulnerability in that product is being actively exploited.

1. VERDICT — YES, THE MANUFACTURER MUST REPORT NOW.

On 17 November 2026 a live obligation under Article 14 of Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 (Cyber Resilience Act) attaches, and the clock starts on awareness. The 2025 placing-on-market date does not postpone or extinguish it.

Three cumulative conditions must hold; each is satisfied here.

(a) Temporal applicability. The CRA entered into force on 10 December 2024 and applies generally from 11 December 2027, but the reporting obligations concerning actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents apply from 11 September 2026 (Commission, Cyber Resilience Act policy page; Commission LEGISUM summary of Reg. 2024/2847; BSI CRA Single Reporting Platform page). 17 November 2026 falls after 11 September 2026, so the obligation is in force. The fact that the substantive product obligations (essential requirements, CE marking, conformity assessment) do not bite until 11 December 2027 is irrelevant: the reporting obligations were expressly carved out and run earlier.

(b) Material scope. The CRA applies to 'products with digital elements' placed on the EU market, regardless of where the manufacturer is based, that connect directly or indirectly to other devices or networks — including IoT/smart-home hardware and software products (Commission LEGISUM summary). Exclusions listed there are: medical devices already covered by specific EU regulations; aviation and automotive products under sector-specific legislation; marine equipment within Directive 2014/90/EU; two- and three-wheel vehicles and quadricycles under Regulation (EU) No 168/2013 (except L1e designed to be pedalled, per Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/1535). A connected consumer product outside that list is in scope.

(c) Threshold. The trigger is an 'actively exploited vulnerability': a vulnerability for which there is reliable evidence that a malicious actor has demonstrably exploited it in a system without the owner's permission (Art. 3(42), as quoted by BSI and ENISA). Two conditions must be met: the vulnerability is present in a product with digital elements, and there is credible evidence of actual exploitation in real-world systems. A published exploit, proof-of-concept code or port scanning is NOT sufficient; a theoretically exploitable but not actively exploited vulnerability is not reportable (BSI). The stated facts assert actual exploitation, so the threshold is met.

Two defences that might have defeated the obligation, and why neither is available:

- Pre-CRA products. Article 14 applies from 11 September 2026 to all products with digital elements falling within the scope of the CRA, including products placed on the market before 11 December 2027 (ENISA SRP FAQ, question 12, citing the Commission's 'FAQs on the CRA Implementation', subsection 5.3). A 2025 placement is therefore no exemption.
- Retrospectivity carve-out. A manufacturer is not required to report retrospectively where it was already aware of the active exploitation before 11 September 2026 (ENISA SRP FAQ, citing Commission FAQs subsections 5.1 and 5.3). Here awareness arose on 17 November 2026, after that date, so the carve-out does not apply — and the obligation applies even where the underlying vulnerability existed or was previously known (ENISA SRP FAQ).

Conclusion on ask 1: the obligation is engaged on 17 November 2026 and the first filing is due within 24 hours.

2. DEADLINES — THE THREE STAGES

| Stage | Legal basis | Statutory clock | Deadline on these facts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Early warning | Art. 14(2)(a) | Without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours of becoming aware of the actively exploited vulnerability | Wednesday 18 November 2026 (same time of day as awareness) |
| Vulnerability notification | Art. 14(2)(b) | Without undue delay and in any event within 72 hours of becoming aware, providing general information and an initial assessment | Friday 20 November 2026 |
| Final report | Art. 14(2)(c) | No later than 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure (e.g. a patch) becomes available | Floating: patch-availability date + 14 days. Worked example: patch released 1 December 2026 → final report due 15 December 2026 |

Sources for the three figures: ENISA Single Reporting Platform FAQ, question 7; BSI CRA Single Reporting Platform page (which anchors them in Art. 14(2) for actively exploited vulnerabilities and Art. 14(3) for severe incidents); European Parliament OEIL procedure summary of Reg. 2024/2847 (early warning within 24 hours; vulnerability notification within 72 hours).

Three points of practice on the deadlines:

- The final report clock is NOT tied to the awareness date. It is triggered by the availability of the remedy or protective measure. Do not wait for the patch before filing the first two: the 24-hour and 72-hour filings are independent and are already running.
- Distinguish the severe-incident track. If the event were classified as a severe incident rather than an actively exploited vulnerability, the final report would be due within 1 month after the 72-hour notification (ENISA; BSI). On the facts given, the AEV track (14 days after the remedy) is the correct one.
- Hours are calendar hours, not business hours. 17 November 2026 is a Tuesday, so 24 hours expires Wednesday 18 November and 72 hours expires Friday 20 November — both ordinary working days, so no extension question arises.

3. WHERE AND HOW TO FILE

Notification goes simultaneously to (i) the CSIRT designated as coordinator and (ii) ENISA, submitted electronically through the CRA Single Reporting Platform (SRP) (Art. 14(1); ENISA SRP FAQ). The coordinating CSIRT is determined primarily by the manufacturer's main place of establishment (Art. 14(7), as described by ENISA); a manufacturer not established in the Union files with the CSIRT of the Member State in which its authorised representative is established — confirm this fallback against the Article 14(7) text before filing. Advance registration is not required and registration plus submission can be completed in a few minutes (BSI). If the SRP is unavailable, the German national fallback is email to CERT-Bund (BSI); check the equivalent fallback published for the relevant coordinating Member State.

Content of the filings:
- Early warning: must indicate, where applicable, the Member States on whose territory the manufacturer is aware the product has been made available, plus the suspected malicious nature of the event (Art. 14(2)(a); EP OEIL summary).
- Vulnerability notification (72h): general information on the vulnerability and an initial assessment of its severity and impact.
- Final report: description of severity and impact, root cause, and applied or ongoing corrective/mitigating measures.
- SRP field set for an AEV includes, where applicable and available: CVE ID, EUVD ID, general information about the vulnerability and exploitation, severity and impact, malicious actor, general nature of the exploit, and Particularly Exceptional Circumstances. Not all fields are mandatory at the 24-hour stage; some become mandatory at 72 hours or in the final report (ENISA).

4. CONSEQUENCES OF MISSING THE DEADLINES

Non-compliance can attract fines of up to 2.5% of the manufacturer's global annual turnover, prohibition or restriction of the product's availability, and withdrawal or recall orders (Commission LEGISUM summary of Reg. 2024/2847). Separately, CSIRTs may themselves inform users of the product where the manufacturer has not done so in a timely manner, if proportionate and necessary (Art. 14(8)), and for a severe incident may inform the public or require the manufacturer to do so after consulting it (Art. 17(2)) (ENISA SRP FAQ).

5. IMMEDIATE ACTION CHECKLIST

T+0 (17 November 2026)
- Open a dated incident record and timestamp the moment of awareness (this fixes all three clocks).
- Evidence the 'reliable evidence of actual exploitation' test: telemetry, exploit artefacts, customer reports, third-party research. Document it, because PoC or scanning alone would not qualify.
- Appoint the Assigned Representative who will file on the SRP; identify affected product versions and the Member States of availability.
- Decide and record the classification: AEV (correct on these facts) versus severe incident.

T+24 hours (by 18 November 2026)
- File the early warning through the SRP, selecting the AEV notification type and listing the Member States of availability.

T+72 hours (by 20 November 2026)
- File the vulnerability notification with general information and an initial severity/impact assessment; state whether a corrective or mitigating measure is in preparation.

Ongoing
- Develop and release the corrective or mitigating measure. On release, start the 14-day final-report clock and diarise it.
- Consider user-facing communication in parallel; do not leave it to a CSIRT to inform users under Art. 14(8).

At remedy + 14 days
- File the final report. Once submitted it generally cannot be edited by the submitter (BSI); only the CSIRT designated as coordinator can close a report (ENISA).

6. EVIDENCE NOTE — HOW THE PROOF OF ABSENCE WAS HANDLED

The harness's proof of absence is expressly scoped to one page: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cyber-resilience-act (7,386 characters). That page states the reporting start date (11 September 2026) but nowhere states the 24-hour, 72-hour or 14-day deadlines. That is a fact about that page only. The answer to ask 2 is not 'that page states none': the three deadlines are printed verbatim on three other pages in the same grounding — the ENISA SRP FAQ (question 7), the BSI CRA-SRP page, and the European Parliament OEIL procedure summary. Ask 2 is therefore answered, and nothing is listed as not stated.

7. ASSUMPTIONS RELIED ON AND LIMITS OF THIS ANALYSIS

- The product is a product with digital elements in scope of the CRA and is not on the exclusion list (medical devices, aviation/automotive, marine equipment, L-category vehicles). If it is excluded — e.g. a medical device under the MDR/IVDR — Article 14 does not apply and the sector regime governs instead (MDR/IVDR vigilance, plus NIS2 and GDPR as applicable).
- The exploitation is actual and evidenced, not merely theoretical.
- The manufacturer remains the responsible economic operator and the product is within its support period.
- The manufacturer is established in the Union, or has an authorised representative in a Member State that determines the coordinating CSIRT.

Parallel regimes: if the manufacturer is also an essential or important entity under Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS2), a separate NIS2 Article 23 early warning (24 hours) and incident notification (72 hours) may run concurrently; if personal data are compromised, the GDPR Article 33 72-hour notification to the supervisory authority applies. A CRA notification does not discharge those obligations.

This is a regulatory analysis of the CRA as published and of the cited official guidance; it is not legal advice, and SRP operational practice may change. Confirm the Article 14(7) fallback rule and the national fallback channel before filing.

The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) aims to make sure all digital products are safe from cyber threats. This rulebook requires that devices and software are designed, updated, and maintained to protect users in our increasingly digital world.
From baby-monitors to smart watches, from apps to computer programs, connectable hardware and software are omnipresent in our daily lives.

These obligations must be met at every stage of the value chain. The CRA also requires manufacturers to handle vulnerabilities during the lifecycle of their products. Some products of particular relevance for cybersecurity may need to undergo a third-party assessment by a notified body before they are sold on the EU market.

quotes.whole:
(a) The sum of the transport indices (TI's) for all packages of Class 7 (radioactive) materials on board a vessel may not exceed the limits specified in Table IIIA of this section.
(b) For freight containers containing packages and overpacks of Class 7 (radioactive) materials, the radiation level may not exceed 2 mSv per hour (200 mrem per hour) at any point on the outside surface and 0.1 mSv per hour (10 mrem per hour) at 2 m (6.6 ft) from the outside surface of the freight container.
(c) The limitations specified in Table IIIA of this section do not apply to consignments of LSA-I material.
(d) The sum of the criticality safety indices (CSI's) for all packages and overpacks of fissile Class 7 (radioactive) materials on board a vessel may not exceed the limits specified in Table IIIB of this section.
(e) Each group of fissile Class 7 (radioactive) material packages and overpacks, containing a sum of CSIs no greater than 50 for a non-exclusive use shipment, or no greater than 100 for an exclusive use shipment, must be separated from all other groups containing fissile material packages and overpacks by a distance of at least 6 m (20 ft) at all times.

verdict.summary:
## Governing requirement
Current edition of IAEA SSR-6 as fetched (ssr-6-2025.pdf). The item is a freight container used as packaging, not under exclusive use, so the TI procedure for a freight container used as packaging and the limit in para. 526(b) apply.

## Calculation
1. Maximum dose rate at 1 m: D = 0.08 mSv/h.
2. Step (a): TI_base = 100 × D = 100 × 0.08 = 8.0.
3. Step (b): Table 7 multiplication factor. Largest cross-sectional area of the load = 3 m². Table 7 bands: ≤1 m² → 1; >1 to ≤5 m² → 2; >5 to ≤20 m² → 3; >20 m² → 10. 3 m² falls in >1 to ≤5 m², so factor = 2.
   TI_unrounded = 8.0 × 2 = 16.0.
4. Step (c): round up to the first decimal place, with ≤0.05 allowed as zero. 16.0 is already at the first decimal place; TI = 16.0.

## Limit check
SSR-6 para. 526(b): for consignments other than those under exclusive use, 'The TI of any freight container used as packaging shall not exceed 50.'
16.0 ≤ 50 → the container is within the TI limit.

The para. 526(a) limit of 10 is for packages/overpacks other than a freight container used as packaging; it is not the applicable limit here. TI 16.0 would exceed 10 if this were an ordinary package, but that is not the case. Table 10 also gives 50 for a freight container not under exclusive use.

## Answer
TI = 16.0 (dimensionless). Yes — within the non-exclusive-use TI limit of 50 for a freight container used as packaging.

## Notes
- The NORM slide deck at https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/21/12/7_transport_of_norm.pdf was searched in full and contains no 'TI limit' / 'maximum TI' wording; it is not the source for the limit and is not used for the verdict. The limit is from SSR-6 para. 526(b).
- This calculation addresses only the TI limit. It does not demonstrate compliance with the separate external-surface dose-rate limit of 2 mSv/h (para. 527) or the 0.1 mSv/h at 2 m conveyance/freight-container limit (para. 566(b)); those require their own measurements.
- The calculation uses 0.08 mSv/h as the maximum at 1 m, as stated in the question. If a higher point value exists, the TI must be recalculated with that maximum.
- The verdict is unchanged if the area factor were not applied (8.0 ≤ 50); however, the current procedure applies the factor for a freight container used as packaging with a 3 m² load, so the stated TI is 16.0.

verdict.summary:
DETERMINATION — RED cybersecurity essential requirements vs. a Bluetooth-connected MDR insulin pump, and date of application of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30

=== 0. ANSWER ===
Ask 1 (verdict): YES. The essential requirements of Article 3(3), points (d), (e) and (f), of Directive 2014/53/EU (RED), as specified by Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30, apply to the Bluetooth-connected insulin pump, even though it is a medical device under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (MDR). The MDR classification confers no exemption; the RED and the MDR apply cumulatively (dual regime).
Condition on which the verdict rests (single decisive fact): the pump's Bluetooth radio is used for communication that reaches the internet, i.e. the pump communicates via the internet through a hub or server (ordinary architecture: BLE pump <-> companion smartphone app <-> manufacturer cloud/server <-> clinician portal). This is the fact pattern assumed in the project brief. If and only if the product were a genuinely closed BLE link to a dedicated local controller with no internet path whatsoever, it would fall outside all three categories of Article 1 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 and the verdict would flip to NO. That exception is not the assumed architecture.
Ask 2 (value): 1 August 2025 (2025-08-01) — the date from which Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 applies to the radio equipment it covers.

=== 1. PRODUCT AND QUESTION ===
Product: infusion/insulin pump, classifiable as a medical device under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (typically class IIb/III, Rule 9/11), incorporating a Bluetooth radio interface used to pair with a controller/companion application and, in normal use, to relay therapy, CGM and status data to a cloud service.
Tasks: (T1) scope determination under the RED as supplemented by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 for Article 3(3)(d),(e),(f); (T2) determination of the date of application of that Delegated Regulation.

=== 2. PRIMARY SOURCES RELIED ON ===
S1. Directive 2014/53/EU (RED), OJ L 153, 22.5.2014 — Article 2(1) (subject matter, definitions: 'radio equipment' = electrical or electronic product which intentionally emits and/or receives radio waves for the purpose of radio communication and/or radio determination, and the product may be completed with an item/accessory such as an antenna); Article 2(2) (exclusions); Article 3(3), points (d) protection of personal data and privacy, (e) protection from fraud, (f) essential features ensuring interoperability with accessories and other equipment, together with the second subparagraph of Article 3(3) empowering the Commission to adopt delegated acts specifying those requirements for specific categories of radio equipment; Article 10/12 (information and instructions, frequency band and max RF power); Annex II (conformity assessment modules). The RED has applied since 13 June 2016.
S2. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 of 29 October 2021 supplementing Directive 2014/53/EU with regard to the application of the essential requirements referred to in Article 3(3), points (d), (e) and (f) of that Directive (CELEX 32022R0030), published in the Official Journal on 29 January 2022. Article 1 lists the categories of radio equipment covered; Article 2 governs entry into force and application.
S3. Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (MDR) — Article 1 and Annex I general safety and performance requirements, in particular Section 17 (electronic programmable systems and software: 17.2 risks arising from negative interaction with the IT environment, 17.3 hardware/IT network characteristics and IT security measures including protection against unauthorised access, 17.4 software lifecycle, verification and validation, state of the art including IT security) and Section 14.2(d) (foreseeable misuse); Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR) where personal data of patients/clinicians is processed by the cloud service.
S4. Harmonised standards supporting Article 3(3)(d),(e),(f): EN 18031-1 (common security requirements — internet-connected radio equipment), EN 18031-2 (radio equipment processing personal data / wearable, childcare and toy equipment), EN 18031-3 (internet-connected radio equipment processing personal and/or traffic data — security provisions). Citation status in the OJ (noted as cited in January 2025, with restrictions on certain clauses that therefore do not give full presumption of conformity) must be re-verified at the moment of application.
S5. Interpretive aids only: Commission 'Blue Guide' (2022/C 247/01) on the interplay of Union product legislation and the possibility of one EU Declaration of Reference covering several acts; Commission guidance on the interplay between the MDR and other Union legislation (radio equipment that is a medical device must satisfy both regimes; one CE marking, covering all applicable acts).
S6. Contrast source: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 (Cyber Resilience Act) expressly excludes products covered by the MDR/IVDR from its scope and applies from 11 December 2027. This is cited to show that the EU legislature created an MDR carve-out where it intended one — and created none in Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30.

=== 3. DECISION PROCEDURE (applicable to any product; applied here) ===
STEP 1 — Is the product 'radio equipment' under Article 2(1) RED?
Finding: YES. A Bluetooth transceiver intentionally emits and receives radio waves for radio communication. The RED definition also covers products that must be completed with an antenna/accessory. Consequence: the RED applies to the pump as a product made available on the market, in parallel with the MDR.

STEP 2 — Does any exclusion in Article 2(2) RED apply?
Exclusions considered: (a) radio equipment used by radio amateurs for non-commercial purposes; (b) marine equipment covered by Union marine legislation; (c) airborne equipment/appliances covered by Union aviation legislation; (d) custom-built evaluation kits used by professionals solely for research and development; (e) equipment used exclusively for activities covered by Chapter II of Common Position 2008/944/CFSP.
Finding: NONE applies. A commercially produced, CE-marked insulin pump is not an amateur-use, marine, airborne, R&D-kit or dual-use-embargo product. NOTE: there is NO medical-device exclusion in Article 2(2).

STEP 3 — Is the pump within a category of Article 1 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30?
Categories of that Article: (a) internet-connected radio equipment; (b) radio equipment communicating via the internet, for example via a hub or server; (c) internet-connected childcare toys and internet-connected toys.
Mapping: the pump pairs over BLE with a smartphone/tablet application which relays data to a manufacturer cloud server. The smartphone acts as the hub; the pump's data therefore travels via the internet through a hub/server -> CATEGORY (b) is satisfied. If a future product connected natively via Wi-Fi/cellular to the internet, category (a) would be satisfied instead. Category (c) is not engaged (not a toy or childcare product).
Finding: COVERED. Decisive fact = existence of an internet communication path (direct or via hub/server). Purely local, closed BLE telemetry with no internet leg would satisfy none of (a),(b),(c) and would be outside the Delegated Regulation.

STEP 4 — Is there a medical-device carve-out or a precedence rule between the RED and the MDR?
Findings:
(i) Article 2(2) RED exclusions do not mention medical devices.
(ii) Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 is inclusionary only: it specifies the categories to which Article 3(3)(d),(e),(f) apply and contains no exclusion, no reference to Regulation (EU) 2017/745, and no clause subordinating it to sectoral product legislation.
(iii) There is no lex specialis clause in the MDR disapplying the RED. The MDR's own cybersecurity-relevant requirements (Annex I Sections 17.2, 17.3, 17.4, 14.2(d)) are parallel obligations on the same device, not a substitute for, and not an exemption from, the RED obligations.
(iv) Contrast: the Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847) does exclude MDR/IVDR products from its scope. The absence of an equivalent exclusion in Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 is deliberate and decisive.
(v) Under general Union product-law practice (Blue Guide), where a product falls under several acts all applicable requirements must be met; the CE marking then attests conformity with all of them.
Finding: NO CARVE-OUT. Dual regime: MDR (medical device) + RED (radio equipment) both apply.

STEP 5 — What substance is triggered?
(d) Protection of personal data and privacy — pump telemetry, glucose and dosing data, identifiers, clinician/patient accounts in the cloud; interlocks with GDPR Art. 25 (data protection by design) and Art. 32 (security of processing).
(e) Protection from fraud — protection of the device identity, of the therapy/alarm data and of the update channel against spoofing, unauthorised reprogramming, counterfeit accessories and fraudulent calls to pay-features/services; the clinical risk of an altered basal/bolus dose is the dominant risk and is assessed jointly under MDR Annex I.
(f) Essential features ensuring interoperability with accessories and other equipment — interoperability with the controller/companion app, CGM/loop components, chargers and accessories, via controlled, secure interfaces (no lock-down that defeats, and no loose interface that breaks, the security model).

STEP 6 — Date of application: see Section 4.

STEP 7 — Conformity/implementation consequences: see Section 5.

=== 4. DATE OF APPLICATION (Ask 2) ===
Instrument: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 of 29 October 2021 (CELEX 32022R0030).
Publication: Official Journal of the European Union, 29 January 2022.
Entry into force: Article 2, first paragraph — the twentieth day following publication = 18 February 2022 (30 January = day 1 … 18 February = day 20).
Date of application: Article 2, second paragraph — the Regulation applies from 1 August 2025.
Consequence: from 1 August 2025 the essential requirements of Article 3(3), points (d), (e) and (f), of the RED apply to the radio equipment falling within the categories of Article 1 of the Delegated Regulation — i.e. to radio equipment that is internet-connected, that communicates via the internet (e.g. via a hub or server), and to internet-connected childcare toys/toys. The Bluetooth insulin pump, covered under category (b) on the assumed architecture, must comply with those requirements for any unit placed on the market or put into service on or after 1 August 2025; equipment lawfully placed on the market before that date remains governed by the regime then in force (subject to national market-surveillance practice).
Amendment check (negative): no amending or postponing act alters 1 August 2025. Specifically: Directive (EU) 2022/2380 (common charger) and Regulation (EU) 2023/607 (MDR transitional provisions for legacy devices) do not touch Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30; Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 (Cyber Resilience Act) applies from 11 December 2027 and does not postpone, replace or repeal the RED delegated act's date of application. Before relying on this formally in a technical file, re-read the consolidated ELI text (eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2022/30) to confirm no subsequent corrigendum or amendment.

=== 5. COMPLIANCE / IMPLEMENTATION PLAN FOR THE MANUFACTURER ===
5.1 Confirm and document the radio architecture (evidence of category (b) or (a)): protocol map BLE <-> app <-> cloud; note that this single fact is what makes the Delegated Regulation applicable.
5.2 Build one consolidated cybersecurity risk and requirements file mapping: RED Art. 3(3)(d) <-> MDR Annex I 17.3/17.4 + GDPR Art. 25/32; RED Art. 3(3)(e) <-> MDR Annex I 14.2(d), 17.2 and clinical risk management (ISO 14971); RED Art. 3(3)(f) <-> accessory/app interface specifications. MDR clinical safety (dose delivery integrity, alarm integrity) remains the dominant risk; the RED adds privacy, fraud-prevention and interoperability obligations.
5.3 Standards route: apply EN 18031-1 (internet-connected radio equipment), EN 18031-2 (personal-data-processing radio equipment, incl. wearables) and EN 18031-3 (interoperability/security provisions) to the extent cited in the OJ without relevant restriction. Where OJ citations carry restrictions on certain clauses, those clauses do not confer presumption of conformity: close them by design evidence, common specifications (if any), or notified-body scrutiny.
5.4 Conformity assessment route under the RED, Annex II:
- Module A (internal production control) only if harmonised standards are applied in full;
- otherwise Module B (EU type-examination) + Module C/D/E, or Module H (full quality assurance);
- the MDR conformity-assessment body (Annex IX/XI) does not certify RED requirements. The RED route must be chosen and, where it requires a notified body, a body designated for Directive 2014/53/EU must be involved. Ensure the RED technical documentation (design, RF, security, update mechanism, penetration/integrity testing) is linked to, or included in, the MDR technical documentation.
5.5 Declaration(s) of conformity: one EU Declaration of Reference may cover both Directive 2014/53/EU (incl. Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 and any harmonised standards used) and Regulation (EU) 2017/745. List all applicable acts and the standards/common specifications applied to each.
5.6 Marking and information: single CE marking; label/instructions to satisfy RED Art. 10/12 (intended use, frequency band(s), maximum transmitted RF power) plus MDR labelling and instructions for use; state the security-relevant user information (pairing, updates, data handling).
5.7 Lifecycle: MDR Annex I 17.4 requires lifecycle-based software development and IT security as state of the art; define secure-update, vulnerability-handling, end-of-support and incident-reporting processes so that both RED post-market obligations (Art. 11/13) and MDR vigilance obligations are met by one procedure.
5.8 Timeline anchor: all of the above must be complete for units placed on the market or put into service on or after 1 August 2025 (2025-08-01). No other compliance date is asserted by this determination.

=== 6. FINAL STATEMENT ===
1) Verdict: YES — the cybersecurity-related essential requirements of Article 3(3)(d), (e) and (f) of Directive 2014/53/EU, as specified by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30, apply to the Bluetooth-connected insulin pump (covered as radio equipment communicating via the internet through a hub/server), and its classification as a medical device under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 does not exempt it; the MDR and RED obligations apply cumulatively.
2) Date: 1 August 2025 (2025-08-01), per Article 2 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30; the Regulation entered into force on 18 February 2022 and has not been postponed or amended.

verdict.summary:
# AC-7 (Unsuccessful Logon Attempts), NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 — what the control actually requires

## 1. Bottom line

**Rev. 5 AC-7 does not require any particular number of attempts, any particular time window, or any particular lockout duration.** All three quantities in the request are *organization-defined parameters* (ODPs) — deliberately blank slots that the control obliges the organization to fill, document in its security plan, and then implement. The control is a requirement to *have* a limit and *have* an automatic response; it is not a source of the numbers themselves.

Consequently, the three asks are resolved as follows, and `results` is intentionally empty because no grounded number exists for any of them:

| Ask | Resolution | Where it lives in the control |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Number of consecutive invalid attempts | **Blocked** — no value in the source | AC-7(a), `[Assignment: organization-defined number]` |
| 2. Time period | **Blocked** — no value in the source | AC-7(a), `[Assignment: organization-defined time period]` |
| 3. Lockout duration | **Not stated** — page states none (proof of absence) | AC-7(b), selection branch `[Assignment: organization-defined time period]`, or no duration at all under the administrator-release branch |

## 2. Verbatim control text (SP 800-53r5, AC-7)

> **AC-7 UNSUCCESSFUL LOGON ATTEMPTS**
> **Control:**
> a. Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; and
> b. Automatically [Selection (one or more): lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; lock the account or node until released by an administrator; delay next logon prompt per [Assignment: organization-defined delay algorithm]; notify system administrator; take other [Assignment: organization-defined action]] when the maximum number of unsuccessful attempts is exceeded.
> **Discussion:** The need to limit unsuccessful logon attempts and take subsequent action when the maximum number of attempts is exceeded applies regardless of whether the logon occurs via a local or network connection. Due to the potential for denial of service, automatic lockouts initiated by systems are usually temporary and automatically release after a predetermined, organization-defined time period. If a delay algorithm is selected, organizations may employ different algorithms for different components of the system based on the capabilities of those components.

Every bracketed item above is an ODP. There is no numeric literal anywhere in AC-7's control text, its discussion, or its Rev. 5 enhancements.

## 3. Where each ask lands, and what fills it

| Ask | Clause | Operation type | Parameter semantics | Filled by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | AC-7(a) | Assignment | Integer count of *consecutive* invalid logon attempts by a user before the AC-7(b) response fires | Organization (SSP / ODP assignment) |
| 2 | AC-7(a) | Assignment | The window within which those attempts must occur to remain "consecutive" (sliding or fixed — the control does not say, so the ODP must) | Organization |
| 3 | AC-7(b) | Selection **and** Assignment | A duration exists only if the first selection branch is chosen; even then it is organization-defined. The second branch ("until released by an administrator") has *no duration by construction*; the third (delay algorithm) is rate limiting, not lockout; the fourth and fifth are notifications/other actions | Organization |

Note the two distinct "time periods" in AC-7: the one in (a) is the **counting window**; the one in (b) is the **lock duration**. They are separate parameters and must be assigned separately — conflating them is the most common error in AC-7 write-ups.

## 4. Evidence that no numbers exist in the source

1. **Control text** — three placeholders, zero literals (§2).
2. **AC-7(1) AUTOMATIC ACCOUNT LOCK** — reads `[Withdrawn: Incorporated into AC-7.]`. The enhancement that a reader might expect to carry lockout specifics is withdrawn and contains no values in Rev. 5.
3. **Discussion** — "automatic lockouts initiated by systems are usually temporary and automatically release after a predetermined, **organization-defined** time period." The publication explicitly refuses to fix the duration.
4. **Full-text proof of absence** — the standard phrasings for a stated lockout duration are absent from the complete 492-page Rev. 5 PDF and from five companion pages read in full (see `not_stated`).
5. **Sibling parameters confirm the pattern** — AC-7(2) mobile-device purge "after [organization-defined number] consecutive, unsuccessful device logon attempts"; AC-7(3) "Limit the number of unsuccessful biometric logon attempts to [organization-defined number]"; AC-7(4) alternate-factor limits, again organization-defined. Every quantitative knob in the AC-7 family is an ODP.

## 5. Caution on circulating figures

Secondary sources — vendor hardening guides, platform security baselines, assessment checklists, and some summary blog posts — do cite concrete attempt counts, windows and lockout durations, and these are sometimes misattributed to AC-7. **They are not in Rev. 5 AC-7**, its withdrawn enhancement (1), or its discussion, per the searches above. Do not cite "NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-7" as the authority for any specific figure in an SSP, a POA&M, an authorization package, or an audit response; cite the actual authority instead (organizational policy, an agency overlay, a control baseline tailoring document, or vendor/STIG guidance). This summary deliberately states no figures, so that nothing here can be quoted as an AC-7 requirement.

## 6. What to do instead — procedure to produce defensible, auditable values

Since the numbers are the organization's to set, the deliverable that actually satisfies AC-7 is a documented parameter assignment plus evidence that the system implements it. Procedure:

**Step 1 — Record the ODPs in the SSP.** Use a table with these columns; one row per parameter:

| Control | ODP identifier | Parameter | Assigned value | Selection made | Rationale | Approving official | Date | Source authority |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AC-7 | (a)-1 | consecutive invalid attempts before response | *assign* | — | *risk rationale* | *name/role* | *date* | *policy / overlay ref* |
| AC-7 | (a)-2 | counting window | *assign* | — | *risk rationale* | *name/role* | *date* | *policy / overlay ref* |
| AC-7 | (b)-1 | automatic response | — | *one or more of the five* | *DoS vs. guessing trade-off* | *name/role* | *date* | *policy / overlay ref* |
| AC-7 | (b)-2 | lock duration (only if branch 1 chosen) | *assign or N/A* | — | *DoS vs. guessing trade-off* | *name/role* | *date* | *policy / overlay ref* |

Take the exact ODP identifiers from the catalog copy you are citing (the OSCAL/800-53B numbering); do not invent them — confirm against the version in hand.

**Step 2 — Choose the values against the risks the control itself names.** The discussion identifies the governing tension: lockouts are a denial-of-service vector, so durations should be bounded and/or paired with a recovery path. Weigh: online-guessing threat, credential-stuffing exposure, availability criticality of the account class, help-desk unlock load, and whether privileged accounts warrant a tighter assignment than standard users (AC-7 permits per-account-class assignments if you document them).

**Step 3 — Make the AC-7(b) selection explicitly.** If you select "lock until released by an administrator," document *how unlock requests are authenticated* (identity proofing, callback, ticket), otherwise the lockout becomes a social-engineering bypass — and note that under that branch ask 3 has no answer because no duration exists. If you select "delay next logon prompt," specify the algorithm and its ceiling. Selections may be combined (the operation is "one or more").

**Step 4 — Define counting semantics inside the ODP so testing is deterministic.** Specify: scope (per account, per account+source, per device — AC-7(2) makes the device-scope distinction explicit); what resets the counter (successful logon, window expiry, administrator unlock); whether the window slides or is fixed; whether the Nth attempt itself triggers the response or the (N+1)th does (state this, because implementers differ); and the clock source (tie to AU-8 timestamps in UTC so the window is testable).

**Step 5 — Reconcile with adjacent controls.** AC-7(2) (mobile-device wipe), AC-7(3) (biometric attempts), AC-7(4) (alternate authentication factor to bypass an inadvertent lockout — the primary mitigation for the DoS concern), IA-5 (authenticator management), AU-2/AU-6 (log and review lockout events), IR-4/IR-6 (handle lockout-driven DoS as an incident), AC-9 (notify the user of unsuccessful attempts since last logon). These do not constrain the AC-7 ODP values but they do constrain the implementation.

**Step 6 — Verify the implementation against the assigned parameters.** Parameterise the test so nothing is hard-coded — the values come from the SSP, which is the point:

```
ODP = { max_attempts: N,        # AC-7(a) assignment
        window: T,              # AC-7(a) assignment
        action: subset of {LOCK_TIMED, LOCK_ADMIN, DELAY, NOTIFY_ADMIN, OTHER},
        lock_duration: D | null # AC-7(b) assignment; null if LOCK_ADMIN chosen
      }

test_limit_and_response(account, ODP):
    # counting-window behaviour: attempts outside T do not accumulate
    for i in 1..(N-1):
        assert login(account, wrong) == REJECTED
        assert account.state == UNLOCKED
    assert login(account, wrong) == REJECTED          # the Nth attempt
    assert response_fired(account, ODP.action)        # limit is N, not N+1

test_lock_duration(account, ODP):
    if LOCK_TIMED in ODP.action:
        trigger_lock(account, ODP.max_attempts)
        assert login(account, correct) == REJECTED while now < lock_start + D
        assert login(account, correct) == ACCEPTED when now >= lock_start + D
    if LOCK_ADMIN in ODP.action:
        trigger_lock(account, ODP.max_attempts)
        assert login(account, correct) == REJECTED indefinitely   # no duration
        admin_unlock(account, authenticated=True)
        assert login(account, correct) == ACCEPTED

test_reset_semantics(account, ODP):
    fail (N-1) times; succeed once; assert counter == 0
    fail (N-1) times; wait > T; fail once; assert account still UNLOCKED

test_accounting(account, ODP):
    assert each invalid attempt and each lock/unlock emits an audit event
           timestamped per AU-8 (UTC), sufficient for AU-6 review
```

Record: configuration export showing N, T, D as configured; test transcript with timestamps; the SSP ODP table. These are the artefacts an assessor will ask for.

**Step 7 — Map to the assessment procedure.** For the AC-7 assessment, cite the AC-7a/AC-7b objectives from SP 800-53A Rev. 5 — but pull the exact objective identifiers from the copy you hold; they were not part of the fetched grounding here and I will not assert them from memory.

## 7. Scope limits and what would unblock the blocked asks

- **No system under assessment was identified**, so this is a statement about the control, not a compliance verdict on any system.
- **SP 800-53B control baselines and any agency overlay** may constrain or pre-assign these ODPs; those documents were not fetched, so no claim is made about them. If the requester supplies the applicable baseline/overlay, or the organization's SSP parameter table, **asks 1 and 2 become answerable directly** — the value is then the assigned parameter, cited to that document, not to AC-7.
- **The premise embedded in the request's assumption block** (that Rev. 5 AC-7 carries specific figures, allegedly from AC-7(1)) is incorrect as to source: AC-7(1) is withdrawn in Rev. 5 and the control contains no literals. Any specific figures must be re-sourced before use.

## 8. One-line answer for a reviewer

AC-7 Rev. 5 requires that the organization *assign* a limit on consecutive invalid logon attempts, *assign* a counting window, and *select* an automatic response (optionally including an *assigned* lock duration, or an administrator release with no duration); it requires no specific number, window, or duration, and the page states no lockout duration.

blocked_on.ask: 1 — What number of consecutive invalid logon attempts
blocked_on.why: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-7 does not state a number. Clause (a) reads 'Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]' — the count is an organization-defined parameter (a blank the organization must fill and document), not a value the publication supplies. No numeric count appears in AC-7's control text, its discussion, or its enhancements in the fetched pages; AC-7(1) AUTOMATIC ACCOUNT LOCK, which would be the natural carrier of such a figure, is marked '[Withdrawn: Incorporated into AC-7.]'. Answering with a number would be answering on paper. The ask becomes answerable once the organization's assigned parameter (from its SSP, an agency overlay, or a baseline tailoring document) is supplied.

Same clause (a): the window is '[Assignment: organization-defined time period]'. Rev. 5 fixes no window. The discussion only says lockouts 'automatically release after a predetermined, organization-defined time period' — again deferring to the organization. No proof of absence exists for this ask, so it is blocked rather than listed as not stated. It becomes answerable when the organization's assigned parameter is supplied.

not_stated.why: The page states no lockout duration. Harness full-text search of https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-53r5.pdf (492 pages, 1,561,656 characters, fetched 2026-11-23T21:52:40Z, sha256 fc63bcd61715) found none of the strings 'lockout duration', 'account lockout duration', 'lockout period', 'time period that the account is locked', or 'duration of the lockout'. The same negative result holds for the five companion pages read in full: the nvlpubs page-parameterised URL (sha256 fc63bcd61715), the OSCAL-derived PDF at csrc.nist.gov (396 pages, 1,287,645 characters, sha256 9ce01f4d67c9), the bsafes AC-7 page (17,836 characters, sha256 f9630cd5ebc4), the alternate-case nvlpubs URL (sha256 fc63bcd61715), and the Rev. 5 draft markup PDF (282 pages, 960,815 characters, sha256 8574eeabc495). Consistent with that, AC-7(b) makes the lock duration a selection: 'lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]' is one option among five, and the option 'lock the account or node until released by an administrator' has no duration by construction. No figure is given here.

The protection of Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) is of paramount importance
to federal agencies and can directly impact the ability of the Federal Government
to successfully conduct its essential missions and functions. This publication provides
organizations with assessment procedures and a methodology that can be used to conduct
assessments of the security requirements in NIST Special Publication 800-171, Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information in Nonfederal Systems and Organizations. The assessment procedures are flexible and can be customized to the needs of organizations

requirements in NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-171, Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) in Nonfederal Systems and Organizations [3]. Organizations can use the assessment procedures to generate evidence that the security
requirements have been satisfied. The scope of the security assessments conducted
using the procedures described in this publication is guided and informed by the system
security plans for systems that process, store, or transmit CUI. The assessment procedures
offer the flexibility to customize assessments based on organizational policies and
requirements, known threat and vulnerability information, system and platform dependencies,

Initial Public Draft (IPD) NIST SP 800-171, Revision 3
Frequently Asked Questions
May 10, 2023
On July 19, 2022, NIST announced its intention to update the series of Special Publications dedicated to
the protection of Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI). We have recently completed the initial
public draft (IPD) of NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-171, Revision 3. The proposed revisions to the
publication have been guided and informed by the public comments received and NIST’s responsibility
to meet the requirements of the Federal Information Security Modernization Act, Executive Order (EO)
13556, CUI federal regulation, and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Circular A-130.
The following frequently asked questions provide background information and rationale for the changes
proposed for NIST SP 800-171, Revision 3:
What are the significant changes between NIST SP 800-171, Revision 2 and Draft NIST SP 800-171,
Revision 3?

• Eliminated the distinction between basic and derived security requirements
• Updated the security requirements and families to reflect updates in the NIST SP 800-53,

quotes.whole: The CUI federal regulation requires federal agencies that use federal information systems to process, store, or transmit CUI to comply with NIST standards and guidelines. The responsibility of federal agencies to protect CUI does not change when the information is shared with nonfederal organizations. Therefore, a similar level of protection is needed when CUI is processed, stored, or transmitted by nonfederal organizations using nonfederal systems, irrespective of the organization’s size. NIST is responsible for developing and publishing the security requirements for the protection of CUI. The application and implementation of the requirements and any compliance issues related to the content of NIST SP 800-171 are the responsibility of the federal agency that has a relationship with a nonfederal organization, as expressed in a specific contract or agreement.

Regularly provide basic and advanced security literacy training to new and existing staff. Customize the content to make it relevant– based on the systems that personnel have authorized access to, contextualized to the work environments of personnel (e.g., telework, shop floor), and tailored to the specific roles of personnel. ✓ How to securely handle CUI (training should be provided to staff before authorizing access to the system or CUI).
✓ How to recognize and report insider threats, social engineering, and social mining.

verdict.summary:
ANSWERS

| # | Ask | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Security requirement families in the current revision (SP 800-171 Rev. 3, Final, 5/14/2024) | **17** |
| 2 | Security requirement families in Revision 2 | **14** |
| 3 | Revision 2's status on NIST's own published copy | **"Withdrawn on May 14, 2024." / "Superseded by SP 800-171 Rev. 3"** |

Status captured 2026-11-23 (fetch timestamps of the NIST pages below). NIST mutates these pages, so the status string is date-stamped.

---

1. CURRENT REVISION = REV. 3 → 17 FAMILIES

Determination of "current": CSRC's SP 800 publications list shows "SP 800-171 Rev. 3 (Final) Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information in Nonfederal Systems and Organizations ... 5/14/2024 Status: Final." No Rev. 4 and no Rev. 3 draft appear in the fetched listings. Rev. 2 is marked withdrawn. Therefore the current revision is Rev. 3.

Count, stated by NIST in its own Rev. 3-era publications (not counted by hand):
- SP 800-171A Rev. 3, Assessing Security Requirements for CUI, May 2024 (Approved by the NIST Editorial Review Board 2024-04-23), §2.1: "The security requirements in SP 800-171 are organized into 17 families, as illustrated in Table 1." — https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/800-171Ar3/NIST.SP.800-171Ar3.html
- NIST SP 1318, Protecting CUI: NIST SP 800-171, Revision 3, Small Business Primer, 8/18/2025: "SP 800-171 security requirements are organized into 17 families, as illustrated in the table below." — https://tsapps.nist.gov/publication/get_pdf.cfm?pub_id=960119

Rev. 3 roster (17): Access Control; Awareness and Training; Audit and Accountability; Configuration Management; Identification and Authentication; Incident Response; Maintenance; Media Protection; Physical and Environmental Protection; Personnel Security; Risk Assessment; Security Assessment and Monitoring; System and Communications Protection; System and Information Integrity; Planning; System and Services Acquisition; Supply Chain Risk Management.

2. REVISION 2 → 14 FAMILIES

Derivation (no fetched page prints the numeral "14" for Rev. 2, so the figure is derived and cross-checked):
- R3 IPD FAQ (May 10, 2023): "Three new security requirement families have been added to Revision 3 ... The families include the Planning (PL) family, the System and Services Acquisition (SA) family, and the Supply Chain Risk Management (SR) family. In addition, the Security Assessment family has been renamed the Security Assessment and Monitoring (SA) family." — https://csrc.nist.gov/files/pubs/sp/800/171/r3/ipd/docs/sp800-171r3-ipd-faq.pdf
- The rename is a rename, not an addition or removal; the only net additions are the three named families. Hence Rev. 2 = 17 − 3 = **14**.
- Arithmetic cross-check: 17 − 14 = 3, exactly the three families the FAQ names. 
- Roster cross-check: Rev. 2 roster AC, AT, AU, CM, IA, IR, MA, MP, PE, PS, RA, CA (Security Assessment), SC, SI = 14; add PL, SA, SR = 17. Consistent.

RECONCILIATION — DO NOT RE-DERIVE 11: The CSRC Rev. 2 page's "Control Families" metadata field reads: "Access Control; Awareness and Training; Audit and Accountability; Configuration Management; Identification and Authentication; Maintenance; Media Protection; Physical and Environmental Protection; Personnel Security; System and Communications Protection; System and Information Integrity" — that is 11 items. It is an incomplete enumeration of the page's metadata, omitting Incident Response, Risk Assessment, and Security Assessment. It is not the Rev. 2 count. Using it as the count would contradict ask 1 (11 + 3 ≠ 17). The correct Rev. 2 figure is 14.

3. REVISION 2'S STATUS ON NIST'S PUBLISHED COPY

Verbatim from NIST CSRC's own Rev. 2 publication page (https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/171/r2/upd1/final):
- "NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 2"
- "Withdrawn on May 14, 2024."
- "Superseded by SP 800-171 Rev. 3"

Supporting metadata on the same page: "Date Published: February 2020 (includes updates as of January 28, 2021)"; Document History: "01/28/21: SP 800-171 Rev. 2 (Final)"; "The PDF of SP 800-171 Revision 2 is the authoritative source of the CUI security requirements" (Planning Note 04/13/2022).

Internal consistency check: the withdrawal date 5/14/2024 is exactly the Rev. 3 publication date shown in the SP 800 list ("SP 800-171 Rev. 3 (Final) ... 5/14/2024 Status: Final"). Withdrawal-on-supersession is coherent.

Net status to report: **Withdrawn (on May 14, 2024) and superseded by SP 800-171 Rev. 3.** Note this is a NIST publication-status designation; it is not a statement that Rev. 2's requirements are void in any given contract. See scope notes.

---

SCOPE NOTES AND CAVEATS (bounding the three values above)

- "Family" = the top-level grouping heading in the SP 800-171 requirement catalog (e.g., Access Control, Incident Response), not individual requirements and not the SP 800-53 control catalog. Both counts use that same definition, which is why they are subtractable.
- Drafts excluded. Rev. 3's Initial Public Draft (and its FAQ) are not the current revision; the Final Rev. 3 (5/14/2024) is.
- Date sensitivity. All three values are as of the 2026-11-23 capture. The status string in particular is mutable; re-verify before relying on it in a filing, SSP, or assessment package.
- Authoritative source. Counts and status are taken from NIST's own publications and CSRC pages, not third-party summaries. Where a numeral was not printed by NIST (Rev. 2's 14), the derivation is shown above so it can be independently reproduced.
- Naming collision to watch downstream: the R3 FAQ uses "(SA)" both for the renamed Security Assessment and Monitoring family and for the new System and Services Acquisition family. Do not treat that as two different counts or as a duplicate family; the roster above disambiguates.
- Compliance context, not an answer change: NIST's own primer states "CMMC is currently based on SP 800-171, Revision 2" even though Rev. 2 is withdrawn on NIST's page. A DFARS/CMMC-driven reader should not assume "withdrawn" means Rev. 2 is no longer the operative baseline in their contract; that determination belongs to the contracting agency, not to NIST's status label.

RE-VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (repeatable, ~5 minutes)
1. Open https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/171/r3/final — confirm Status: Final and the date; record it.
2. Open https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/171/r2/upd1/final — copy the status line verbatim ("Withdrawn on ...", "Superseded by ...") and record the capture date alongside it.
3. Confirm the family count from the Rev. 3 SP 800-171A §2.1 sentence ("organized into 17 families"), not from any metadata field.
4. Recompute Rev. 2 as Rev. 3 count minus the number of families the Rev. 3 transition FAQ names as added; confirm the subtraction equals the number of named additions. If NIST ever publishes a Rev. 4, redo step 3 and step 4 against the new FAQ.

Cyber Resilience Act
The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) aims to make sure all digital products are safe from cyber threats. This rulebook requires that devices and software are designed, updated, and maintained to protect users in our increasingly digital world.
From baby-monitors to smart watches, from apps to computer programs, connectable hardware and software are omnipresent in our daily lives. Less apparent to many users is the security risk such products may present.
The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) aims to safeguard consumers and businesses buying software or hardware products with digital elements. The CRA addresses the inadequate level of cybersecurity in many products, and the lack of timely security updates. It also tackles the challenges consumers and businesses currently face when trying to determining which products are cybersecure and in setting them up securely, making it easier to identify hardware and software with the proper cybersecurity features.

quotes.whole:
The CRA introduces mandatory cybersecurity requirements for manufacturers, covering the planning, design, development and maintenance of such products. These obligations must be met at every stage of the value chain. The CRA also requires manufacturers to handle vulnerabilities during the lifecycle of their products. Some products of particular relevance for cybersecurity may need to undergo a third-party assessment by a notified body before they are sold on the EU market.
Products will bear the CE marking to indicate that they comply with the CRA requirements and national market surveillance authorities will ensure enforcement of the rules.
The CRA entered into force on 10 December 2024. The main obligations introduced by the Act will apply from 11 December 2027, with reporting obligations to apply as of 11 September 2026.
On 27 July 2026, the Commission published practical guidance to help manufacturers, developers, and businesses of all sizes meet their obligations under the Cyber Resilience Act.
The Cyber Resilience Act builds on the 2020 EU Cybersecurity Strategy and EU Security Union Strategy. It complements other legislation in this area, specifically the NIS2 Directive.

quotes.whole:
What is the Cyber Resilience Act?
The Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, known as the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), is a horizontal regulatory framework of the European Union (EU), which applies to hardware and software products (“products with digital elements”) that are made available on the Union market. Such products include both final products and components placed separately on the market.
It aims to set the conditions for the development of secure hardware and software in the Union, in order to strengthen the EU approach to cybersecurity and improve the functioning of the internal market. It also empowers users to take cybersecurity into account when buying and using such products by ensuring that adequate information is made available to them.
The CRA entered into force on 10 December 2024. It will be fully applicable as of 11 December 2027 with some provisions starting to apply earlier: Chapter IV on the notification of conformity assessment bodies will apply from 11 June 2026, whereas reporting obligations set out in Article 14 apply from 11 September 2026.

quotes.whole:
‘Actively exploited vulnerability’ means a vulnerability for which there is reliable evidence that a malicious actor has exploited it in a system without permission of the system owner (CRA definition).
‘Incident having an impact on the security of the product with digital elements’ means an incident that negatively affects (or is capable of negatively affecting) the ability of a product with digital elements to protect the availability, authenticity, integrity or confidentiality of data or functions (CRA definition).
Manufacturers and, once applicable, open-source software stewards must adhere to the following reporting deadlines:
Early Warning: Without undue delay and in any case within 24 hours of becoming aware of the actively exploited vulnerability or severe incident;
Actively Exploited Vulnerability/Severe Incident Notification: Without undue delay and in any case within 72 hours of becoming aware, providing general information and an initial assessment;
Final Report:
For actively exploited vulnerabilities: No later than 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure (e.g., patch) becomes available.
For severe incidents: Within 1 month after the 72-hour notification.

Entry into force and application
Key dates

Article 14 of the Cyber Resilience Act creates two reporting duties for manufacturers of products with digital elements. They are narrower than they first appear: routine bugs and ordinary patches are not in scope. Art. 14
Actively exploited vulnerabilities; a vulnerability in your product for which there is reliable evidence that a malicious actor has exploited it in a system without the owner's permission. A vulnerability you discover and patch before it is exploited is handled through your normal vulnerability-handling process, not this reporting channel.

This is the part that catches people out, and it is worth being exact about. Article 69(2) sets the general transitional rule: products placed on the market before 11 December 2027 fall under the Regulation only if they are substantially modified from that date.
